In summary, offering team members the ability to work remotely is a strong business decision. But it is also fundamentally a better and necessary way for society to operate.
Lastly, for businesses, remote work is the most effective way to build the diverse team you need to win.

(I’m a big fan of geographic and family-based community. Ideological communities, like those formed by people who want similar careers or who want to build similar products, are great but insufficient. Ideological communities alone are echo chambers.)

For communities, remote work helps people visit and return to places they’re already invested in, or maybe even never move in the first place. And that means more time spent with different kinds of people.
For individuals, remote work enables more choice and living on your own terms.

Enter remote work: Flexibility to unbundle key career decisions from personal decisions.
Like where to live, or whether you can take time to care for family.
Even if you’re building a pure software product—especially if you’re building a pure software product, you should be spending time with people outside of tech.
And that’s how the most influential products are made by people who mostly hang out with similar people, who mostly work in the same industry. Not a good situation.

If you’re interested in tech today, there’s an incredibly strong pull to SF, NY (& Miami?). A lot of people like me move to invest in our careers.
One of the easiest ways to make friends when you’re new and young? Colleagues at work, and their friends.

- Focus on content not faces
- Hide your own video
- Walk around
- Shift why you talk from executing to bonding & ideating
- Unschedule your mtgs -> talk when you feel like it

@jornvandijk The different decisions play off each other in nuanced ways. For example Paper is great for collaborative, high trust teams, but falls short with maintaining top-down structure. Notion is better at helping someone central organize the team's content.

@jornvandijk Teams that "want to be friends" will use social tools like Donut, icebreakers, or in general tools with more emojis 🙂

@jornvandijk Writing-first teams tend to use long-form tools like email/Notion/Paper.

Video-first teams either have more video calls or use tools like Loom to record video.

@jornvandijk More consensus-driven teams need a high meeting load or put decision making in structured tools like Jira; maybe GDocs / Paper.

More decentralized teams have decisions made locally. Maybe documented in PRs, Figma, etc. FYI'd in Slack/Email.

@jornvandijk I’d start by thinking about what kind of remote culture the team wants, then find tools to fill gaps.

Example choices:
- async vs face-to-face
- include everyone on decisions vs decentralized autonomy
- writing first vs video first
- high/low trust
- friends or just colleagues
